segments.text: When you ask an AI a question, it first works out what your words mean together.
But once it understands your prompt, how does it actually begin its reply?
Let's look at a simple example.
What should I name my new dog?
This board shows how the process starts.
First, the AI breaks your question down into smaller pieces, called tokens.
Then it assigns positions, which marks exactly where each piece belongs in the sentence.
Next, it turns these tokens into numbers,
starting vectors that carry their initial meaning.
As this information passes through the model's layers,
attention mechanisms update those numbers,
using context from the entire message.
The entire reading process builds toward the end of the prompt.
The AI relies on this final token's updated numbers
to predict what word comes next.
This board isolates that exact transition point.
The moment reading becomes writing.
We are looking at how the AI prepares to generate the very first word of its response.
The final token acts as a funnel.
The question mark gathers information from every single token before it.
The AI takes this specific final token's updated vector
and uses it to calculate a probability score for every possible word.
That single token is the launching pad,
providing the exact mathematical information needed to predict a fitting first token.
The AI is now ready to reply.
It uses those numbers from the final token
to calculate a probability score for every potential next token in its entire vocabulary.
This triggers a repeating generation loop.
The AI selects a token, adds it to the growing reply,
and then uses that newly expanded context to predict again.
Let's look at prediction one on the left.
Because the reply hasn't started yet,
the AI is solely using the question mark as its final context token.
The top predictions for this first slot are u at 18%,
a at 14%, and great at 9%.
In this instance, the AI selects u to start the sentence.
Following the arrow to the right,
three subsequent prediction cycles occur.
The AI runs the loop repeatedly,
smoothly adding the tokens could name and him to the sequence.
Arriving at prediction five in the top right,
our context has now grown to read you could name him.
This means the word him,
acts as the new final token to launch the next prediction.
Based on this longer context,
the top predictions shift significantly.
Down below, we see spot at 22%,
max at 17%, and buddy at 14%.
The AI selects spot to complete the thought.
The completed sequence forms a full sentence.
You could name him spot.
You might notice a slight disconnect here.
We specifically asked for a dog name,
yet the AI started its answer with the word you.
It did this because you is a highly probable,
natural way to begin conversational text,
even before the specific subject of the dog is introduced.
Each added token changes what can fit next.
It is only after the sequence you could name him is established
that a specific dog name becomes the statistically obvious next choice.
The loop doesn't go on forever.
AI keeps predicting tokens until it produces a special token
that signals the answer is finished.
This repeating cycle has a formal name, inference.
In step one, rank.
The AI scores every possible next token,
just like we saw with the 22%, 17% and 14% probability scores for dog names.
In step two, pick.
The AI makes a mathematical selection from those rankings,
exactly as it picked spot.
Next is step three, add.
The selected token is physically attached to the growing answer sequence.
Finally, step four is repeat.
The AI takes this newly lengthened context
and asks the model to predict all over again.
Pulling back, we can see the complete system.
Every answer is built one token at a time.
The whole run is called inference.
